title: Constant-time maximum with restoration
stem: A stack S supports PUSH, POP and TOP. Design FIND-MAX(S) to return the largest currently stored value efficiently. Which proposed approach is correct and efficient?
options: Maintain one MAX variable on PUSH. FIND-MAX is constant time, but rebuilding MAX after a POP needs linear time.
Each FIND-MAX pops all elements, computes the maximum, and restores the original order. Each query is linear.
On every PUSH, an auxiliary stack M stores the maximum of the prefix then present in S. A POP also removes M's top. FIND-MAX is constant time.
On every PUSH, recursively compute the maximum of the current stack and append it to S. FIND-MAX takes logarithmic time.
solution: Option 3 stores one cached maximum per data-stack prefix. Induction proves each M entry is the maximum of the corresponding S prefix; synchronous POP exposes the prior valid prefix. PUSH, POP, TOP of M and FIND-MAX all use constant operations, and M uses O(n) space. Duplicates are retained because every push stores a prefix result. Option 1 explicitly needs a linear rebuild after removing the current maximum, so it does not give the same complete efficient interface. Option 2 preserves the answer and order only with restoration storage but scans on every query. Option 4 adds metadata as if it were data and gives no valid logarithmic recurrence. Empty-stack maximum must have a specified error/identity policy. This is an independently derived answer, not an official key.

title: Doubly linked deque end costs
stem: A deque is implemented using a doubly linked list. Enqueue and dequeue can occur at either end. Which complexity statement is correct? Assume the endpoint handles required by this representation are available.
options: All insertion and removal operations at either end take O(n).
Only front removal takes O(1), while all other operations take O(n).
All insertion and removal operations at either end take O(1).
Rear insertion and front removal take O(1), but rear removal takes O(n).
solution: With direct endpoint access, insertion connects a new node with its endpoint neighbor and updates the endpoint or sentinel links. Removal uses both successor and predecessor fields to reconnect neighbors, including the empty/singleton cases. Each action changes a constant number of fields, so option 3 is correct under the standard unit-cost allocation/payload model. Option 4 describes the predecessor limitation of a singly linked queue, which does not apply to a doubly linked deque. A list without endpoint handles would require locating an end; the English adaptation makes the conventional exam assumption explicit rather than hiding it.

title: Removing dominated rear elements
stem: A doubly linked list Q stores numbers and has first/last handles. Delete(k) removes the first k elements in order. Append(c) repeatedly deletes the last element while it is greater than c, then inserts c at the rear. Starting empty, n such calls are made in any order. Which listed upper bound applies to total cost under one unit per individual node insertion/deletion?
solution: Let a be the number of Append calls. Every node is created by one of these calls and can be deleted at most once, either by a later rear-dominance step or by Delete. Total individual insertions are a<=n; deletions are at most a. Therefore node primitives are at most 2a<=2n, giving the listed 2n bound. The logical Delete(k) must be legal (k no greater than length), or have a declared clamp policy. A sharper all-Append adversarial sequence has n insertions and n-1 deletions, totaling 2n-1; lower-bound scanning/guard costs modify constants but keep Theta(n). Option n undercounts insertion plus deletion work in such a sequence. The symbol k in option 1 cannot describe all calls with varying k. The original question compresses the unit model; this solution states it explicitly.
